extra.message: In Student.create, the user-controlled `name` argument (sourced from POST data['name'] in the students view at sqli/views.py:57) is interpolated into the SQL string via Python %-formatting (`VALUES ('%(name)s') % {'name': name}`) and the resulting string is executed via cur.execute(q) with no parameterization. An attacker can submit a name such as `x') RETURNING id; -- ` to inject arbitrary SQL and read or modify data. This endpoint is reachable without authentication.

Jinja2 is initialized with autoescape=False, so every `{{ }}` interpolation renders raw HTML. User-controlled values (student names, course title/description, and review_text) are output without escaping in the templates (e.g. course.jinja2 lines 14-15 and 22, courses.jinja2 lines 17-18, students.jinja2 line 16), enabling stored XSS. A user who creates a course/review/student containing a `<script>` payload executes JavaScript in every visitor's browser.

The csrf_middleware is implemented (sqli/middlewares.py:26) but is commented out of the application middleware list (line 27: `# csrf_middleware,`). As a result every state-changing POST handler (login, create student/course, evaluate, review, logout) has no CSRF protection, allowing cross-site request forgery. The templates still emit _csrf_token fields, confirming protection was intended.

The evaluate handler writes marks via Mark.create on POST but has no @authorize decorator and no authentication/authorization check. The template only renders the evaluate form for `auth_user.is_admin` (course.jinja2 line 41), indicating an admin-only action. Any client can POST directly to /students/{student_id}/evaluate/{course_id} without logging in to assign arbitrary marks.

The courses handler creates courses via Course.create on POST but has no @authorize decorator and no authentication/authorization check. The template only shows the create form when `auth_user and auth_user.is_admin` (courses.jinja2 line 25), indicating admin-only intent. Any client can POST directly to /courses/ without logging in to create courses.

The students handler creates students via Student.create on POST with no authentication check. The template only renders the form for logged-in users (`{% if auth_user %}`, students.jinja2 line 21), indicating authentication is intended. An unauthenticated attacker can POST directly to /students/ to create students and reach the SQL-injectable Student.create sink.

cwe: CWE-306: Missing Authentication for Critical Function

extra.message: The session storage is constructed with httponly=False (RedisStorage(app['redis'], httponly=False)), so the session cookie is exposed to JavaScript via document.cookie. Combined with the stored-XSS vulnerabilities (autoescape disabled), this lets an attacker steal session cookies and hijack sessions.

check_password verifies credentials by comparing the stored hash to md5(password).hexdigest() with no salt and no key stretching. MD5 is fast and cryptographically broken, so password hashes (including the fixtures md5('password') and md5('superadmin')) can be recovered near-instantly via rainbow tables or brute force. A salted slow KDF (bcrypt/argon2) should be used instead.

cwe: CWE-916: Use of Password Hash With Insufficient Computational Effort
CWE-327: Use of a Broken or Risky Cryptographic Algorithm

extra.message: The aiohttp Application is created with debug=True. In debug mode the server emits detailed error pages with stack traces and internal state (the 50x template even dumps error.__dict__), leaking source paths, configuration details, and other sensitive internals to attackers.

Database credentials (user=postgres, password=postgres) are hard-coded in config/dev.yaml. This file is the default config used by run.py and is the config mounted in docker-compose, so the deployed service uses these credentials. Hard-coded credentials in version control risk unauthorized database access.

The DB seed fixture creates an enabled administrator account with a known username and password (username='superadmin', pwd_hash=md5('superadmin'), is_admin=TRUE). Dockerfile.db copies migrations/* into /docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/, so these fixtures are loaded automatically on first database init, giving anyone who knows the default credentials full administrative access.
